lesson.title: Measuring the Wobble: How Standard Error Quantifies Uncertainty
lesson.summary: The standard error is the standard deviation of a sampling distribution, and it measures how much a statistic typically varies from sample to sample.
lesson.body:
Every interval estimate needs a way to measure how much cushion is reasonable, and that measurement is the standard error. Formally, the standard error is just the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic, the same quantity from earlier chapters on the sampling distributions of p-hat and x-bar, but now used for a specific practical purpose: quantifying the typical distance between a sample statistic and the parameter it estimates.

For a sample proportion, the standard error is the square root of p-hat times (1 minus p-hat), divided by n. Notice this uses p-hat, the sample proportion, in place of the true p, because in real inference problems p is exactly what is unknown, so the best available substitute is used. For a sample mean, the standard error is sigma divided by the square root of n, when the population standard deviation sigma is known, or s divided by the square root of n, using the sample standard deviation, when sigma is not known, a substitution which, for more advanced work, leads to using the t-distribution instead of the normal distribution, a refinement covered later.

Standard error shrinks as sample size n grows, because both formulas divide by a function of n. This matches intuition: a larger sample gives a more stable, less variable estimate of the parameter. It is also why standard error, not the raw spread of individual data points, is the right ingredient for building an interval estimate. An interval estimate is about how precisely we have pinned down the parameter using this whole sample, not about how spread out individual observations happen to be.

For the transit survey, p-hat equals 0.25 from a sample of n equals 400. The standard error is the square root of (0.25 times 0.75) divided by 400, which is the square root of 0.1875 divided by 400, or the square root of 0.00046875, which equals approximately 0.0217. This means that if the survey were repeated many times with new random samples of 400 adults, the resulting sample proportions would typically differ from the true population proportion by about 0.0217, or 2.17 percentage points.

For contrast, consider a bottling plant filling bottles with a known process standard deviation of sigma equals 10 milliliters. A random sample of 50 bottles has a mean fill of x-bar equals 500 milliliters. The standard error of the sample mean is 10 divided by the square root of 50, which is 10 divided by about 7.0711, or approximately 1.4142 milliliters. This standard error is the raw ingredient the next chapter uses to compute a margin of error for both examples.
